.@OpenRouter co-founder Alex Atallah on personal agents: 10 specialized chiefs of staff beat one universal agent. One job each means you can see exactly where it's failing.

"The worst part about doing cross-domain joins with your personal agent is that the more work you give it, the more understanding of what's going on you're sacrificing."

"And no one is taking responsibility for that sacrifice. Agents don't have any responsibility."

"With a universal agent that's doing all things, I can't adjust how much understanding I'm sacrificing."

"It points me towards: maybe down the road, the sub-agents people use will be very vertically focused, and we have a chief of staff type agent that coordinates between them."

"You need vertically focused agents where this agent is more responsible, psychologically, for these things. I want quality checks that make sure it's doing those things correctly. It doesn't need to focus on anything else, it has one focus area."

"I wonder if that's going to help people get at least a loose sense of responsibility on top of agents."

@alexatallah

.@OpenRouter co-founder Alex Atallah, in his first podcast since Stripe acquired the company, joins @Replit co-founder Amjad Masad and a16z's Erik Torenberg on why the future of AI is independence and specialization.

In this conversation, Alex walks through how the Stripe deal unfolded, why he wasn't originally looking to sell, and why "payments and inference are going to blend together."

Pre-OpenRouter, the typical AI workflow had one model provider to choose from, and little pressure on that provider to lower prices. Now enterprises are diversifying across labs and open-weight models, and every board is asking about AI costs and benchmarks.

Amjad argues if your company depends on one AI lab, it can turn into your competitor. So Replit is building the layer that lets enterprises use any model and any cloud, without being locked into either.

Alex and Amjad are split on personal agents – Amjad runs one agent across his whole company and loves the cross-domain joins, while Alex says general agents cause you to sacrifice understanding, and argues 10 specialized chiefs of staff beats one superagent.

Wall Street is going nearly 24 hours. Nasdaq launches an overnight session in December, and the all-night exchange is next.

So who actually trades the overnight tape? SEC data has the answer, and it is not the big institutions.

In the overnight window, 8pm to 4am, foreign accounts are the single largest slice of volume, with dealers and prop traders filling much of the rest. Long-only institutions almost sit it out until regular hours open.

That matters for anyone tempted to trade at 2am. The overnight session is the thinnest, least institutional part of the day. That means less liquidity, wider spreads, and prices that gap on small orders.

As trading goes around the clock, know that the graveyard shift is where liquidity is worst, not where the smart money is deepest.

A lesson in why debt data credibility is everything.

Gabon's dollar bond yields just surged toward 14%, right as the country lines up new borrowing. In July it already paid 12.65% to issue, the highest yield on any emerging-market government deal this year.

A government audit now claims Gabon's public debt is smaller than previously reported, nearly a fifth lower. Normally less debt is good news.

But the audit has not been published. The market is pricing a number it has not seen, with no methodology and no detail on what got reclassified away. A debt pile that shrinks in the dark reads as data risk, not relief.

In sovereign credit, trust is the collateral. When the numbers move and the story is not shown, yields go up, not down.

Paramount just borrowed $52 billion to buy Warner Bros. One of the largest debt deals ever. The finale was hair-raising.

The stack: $30B in investment-grade bonds, $12.4B in junk, and about $9.5B in loans. Blue-chip and junk stapled together to fund one mega-merger.

Then the crack showed up in duration. Investor orders for Paramount's longest-dated bonds vanished between peak demand and final pricing. It lost more than half the book on its 20, 30, and 40-year bonds.

The bond market will fund a jumbo deal. It will not lend to a levered media company for 40 years without flinching. The long end nearly broke, and the bonds slumped once they started trading.

Duration is where the demand dies now.

Hedge funds just gave up on the yen. Again.

For a brief window, leveraged funds flipped net long the yen, their first bullish bet in ages. Then they erased it and rebuilt shorts, turning net bearish into the end of September.

The carry trade is back on. Borrow the cheap, low-yielding yen, buy higher-yielding everything else, and pocket the spread.

Remember what this trade did in August 2024. A crowded yen short is a loaded spring. When the yen rallies hard, the unwind is violent and it does not stay in Tokyo. It lands on global stocks.

The more one-sided this gets, the harder the eventual snap.

When a company says its market is the size of the entire US economy, hold onto your wallet.

Anthropic is reportedly telling IPO investors its total addressable market tops $30 trillion. SpaceX pitched $28.5 trillion. The entire US economy is about $32 trillion.

TAM is the revenue you would earn if you captured 100% of a market you drew yourself. It is the easiest number in finance to inflate.

History gives the warning. WeWork claimed a giant addressable market right before it imploded. The bigger the TAM slide, the bigger the red flag.

Treat a TAM the size of US GDP as a sentiment signal, not a valuation input. Right now the slides are getting loud.
